title: Getting Your Guidance Weights Right in diffusion and flow-matching posterior sampling

paper.title: Getting Your Guidance Weights Right in diffusion and flow-matching posterior sampling
paper.abstract:
Abstract Training-free posterior sampling methods, also known as Plug-and-Play methods, leverage pretrained unconditional diffusion or flow-matching models to solve inverse problems. Most existing approaches rely on guidance weights to balance, at each time step, prior information from the unconditional score or velocity network with measurement consistency, yet the tuning of these weights is often not discussed and is largely left to heuristics.
We introduce a simple and principled offline strategy for automatically tuning these guidance weights. Our key observation is that, at each time step, the conditional denoising score-matching objective for diffusion models, or the conditional flow-matching objective for flow-matching models, is a least-squares objective. Therefore, when the conditional prediction is expressed as a weighted sum of the unconditional network output and a measurement-guidance term, optimizing over these weights reduces to a two-dimensional linear least-squares problem.
The resulting time-dependent guidance weights can be optimized offline for a given measurement operator, noise level and sampler at the cost of a single minibatch of sampling trajectories,
without retraining or fine-tuning the pretrained generative model.
Instantiated with the standard Tweedie-based measurement-consistency term, our approach improves posterior sampling and achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction performance across diffusion- and flow-matching-based methods. Moreover, the optimized guidance weights enable diffusion samplers to reduce the number of sampling steps from 1000 to 50 with no significant degradation in reconstruction quality.
Code will be made available.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Karras et al., 2022 ; Song & Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020 ; Song & Ermon, 2020 ) and flow matching models ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu, 2022 ; Tong et al., 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) have emerged as dominant families of iterative generative models, achieving remarkable success in synthesizing high-fidelity samples across a wide range of data modalities. However, training these models remains computationally expensive and can require substantial computational resources and time. In inverse problems, where the exact measurement operator and noise characteristics often depend on the acquisition setting specified at inference time, retraining or fine-tuning a generative model for each new acquisition setting is often impractical. Practitioners instead commonly rely on training-free methods ( Chung et al., 2022a ; Song et al., 2023 ; Boys et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Martin et al., 2025 ) , also referred to as Plug-and-Play methods. These methods leverage unconditionally pretrained generative models to perform approximate posterior sampling without requiring additional training for different measurement operators or noise levels. Most existing training-free methods ( Chung et al., 2022a ; Song et al., 2023 ; Boys et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Martin et al., 2025 ) incorporate a measurement-consistency step at each time step to modify the unconditional sampling direction, thereby steering the sampling trajectory toward samples consistent with the measurement. Repeating this procedure throughout the sampling process yields a sample from the approximate posterior distribution. Such methods usually rely on guidance weights to balance, at each time step, the prior information provided by the unconditional score or velocity network against measurement consistency. However, the tuning of these weights is often not discussed and is largely left to heuristics. In practice, the measurement setup may frequently change, for instance by modifying the number or locations of sensors, or their internal acquisition settings ( Donoho, 2006 ) . Such modifications require the guidance weights to be re-tuned, introducing an additional and time-consuming hyperparameter optimization step. Consequently, the need to tune guidance weights represents a key practical bottleneck of existing training-free posterior sampling methods. This motivates the development of a strategy to automatically and efficiently determine appropriate guidance weights for a given measurement setup. Importantly, such a strategy must introduce negligible computational overhead. From a practitioner’s perspective, guidance selection should take only a few seconds, ruling out iterative optimizers ( e.g. gradient descent, etc.) that require repeated ODE/SDE integrations. In this paper, we introduce a simple and principled offline calibration strategy for automatically tuning time-dependent guidance weights. Our contributions are as follows: • We make the key observation that, at each time step, the conditional denoising score-matching objective for diffusion models and the conditional flow-matching objective for flow-matching models are least-squares objectives. Therefore, when the conditional prediction is expressed as a weighted sum of the unconditional network output and a measurement-guidance term, optimizing these weights reduces to a two-dimensional linear least-squares problem. This yields a highly efficient, simulation-free strategy for calibrating time-dependent guidance weights. • While theoretically grounded, the simulation-free calibration strategy does not guarantee improved posterior sampling trajectories, since neither the measurement-consistency term nor the unconditional network is necessarily optimal. To address this limitation, we propose a greedy SIMulation-based CAlibration strategy (SIMCA), which sequentially calibrates the guidance weight at each time step while keeping the weights calibrated at previous time steps fixed. SIMCA requires only a single minibatch of sampling trajectories, making it practical for tuning time-dependent guidance weights in a given measurement setup. • We empirically demonstrate that SIMCA, instantiated with the standard Tweedie-based measurement-consistency term, matches or surpasses state-of-the-art training-free methods across multiple inverse problems and datasets, using both diffusion and flow-matching backbones. • We further show that SIMCA enables diffusion samplers to reduce the number of sampling steps from 1000 to 50, a × 20 \times 20 reduction in inference cost, without significant degradation in reconstruction quality.

sections.heading: Guidance weights in training-free posterior sampling.
sections.text: Additive training-free samplers weight their measurement-consistency term either heuristically, as the residual-normalized step of DPS ( Chung et al., 2022a ) and the hand-set schedules of flow-based samplers ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Martin et al., 2025 ) , or through a Gaussian model of the denoising posterior, as in Π \Pi GDM ( Song et al., 2023 ) , TMPD ( Boys et al., 2023 ) , their refinements ( Peng et al., 2024 ) , and their flow counterpart OT-ODE ( Pokle et al., 2024 ) . The latter derive the weight from an assumed posterior covariance rather than tuning it, and thereby improve both the measurement term and its effective scale; our ablations suggest that this second effect accounts for much of their benefit (Section 5.3 ). What none of them does is fit the weight to a criterion measurable from data, and all fix the weight of the pretrained field to one.

sections.heading: Adaptive guidance.
sections.text: Time-varying weights have been studied mainly for classifier-free guidance ( Malarz et al., 2025 ) , where the weight trades sample quality against conditioning fidelity and, having no reference value, is set heuristically. In training-free inverse problems the guided field approximates a well-defined conditional field, so its approximation error can be measured against the tractable target of Eq. 5 and minimized in closed form rather than tuned. SAIP ( Wang & Meng, 2026 ) also adapts the balance between the two terms, but through a single coupled parameter, estimated online and stated against the intractable posterior score. Methodologically, our closed-form solve from Monte Carlo moments follows Analytic-DPM ( Bao et al., 2022 ) , applied there to the unconditional reverse variance.

sections.heading: Cost.
sections.text: SIMCA requires only a single minibatch of sampling trajectories, making it practical for tuning time-dependent guidance weights for a given measurement setup. Once calibrated, the guidance weights are fixed and introduce no inference-time overhead.

sections.heading: Recalibration.
sections.text: The guidance weights depend on the measurement operator 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , the noise level σ m \sigma_{m} , the measurement-consistency term 𝐟 \mathbf{f} , the pretrained unconditional network 𝐮 𝜽 \mathbf{u}_{\bm{\theta}} , the sampler Φ \Phi , and the number of timesteps. They must therefore be recomputed whenever any of these components changes. Since each recalibration requires only one offline pass, practitioners can efficiently adapt the guidance weights to different measurement setups.

sections.heading: Compatibility.
sections.text: Our calibration procedure applies to any method whose guidance takes the additive form in Eq. equation 8 . It requires no retraining, architectural changes, or modifications to the sampler.

sections.heading: Backbones and protocols.
sections.text: To fairly evaluate SIMCA, we follow the evaluation protocols of DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) for diffusion and Flower ( Pourya et al., 2026 ) for flow matching. See Appendix F for further details.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: For diffusion we compare against DPS ( Chung et al., 2022a ) , DDRM ( Kawar et al., 2022a ) , DDNM ( Wang et al., 2022 ) , DiffPIR ( Zhu et al., 2023 ) , FPS-SMC ( Dou & Song, 2024 ) , and DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . For flow matching we compare against PnP-GS ( Hurault et al., 2022 ) , DiffPIR ( Zhu et al., 2023 ) , OT-ODE ( Pokle et al., 2024 ) , D-Flow ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ) , Flow-Priors ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , PnP-Flow ( Martin et al., 2025 ) , and Flower ( Pourya et al., 2026 ) . All baseline metrics are those published by the respective benchmarks, obtained under the same operators, noise levels, and test images as ours, with hyperparameters grid-searched to maximize PSNR.

sections.heading: Calibration protocol.
sections.text: Guidance weights are calibrated offline on images disjoint from the test images: for flow matching, we use the same calibration split as in ( Pourya et al., 2026 ) ; for diffusion, we use images from the training sets of FFHQ ( Karras et al., 2019 ) and ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) . All main tables report SIMCA, the simulation-free variant being deferred to Section 5.3 . Since the weights are tied to the sampler and its discretization, each configuration is calibrated separately and its step count reported: K ∈ { 1000,500 , 50 } K\in\{1000,500,50\} for diffusion, with a finer sweep in Appendix E , and the renoising sampler of Flower (with the same number of steps) or a plain Euler integrator for flow matching.

sections.heading: Effect of the step count.
sections.text: The three SIMCA rows in each block of Table 1 differ only in the number of sampler iterations. Surprisingly, halving the budget from 1000 1000 to 500 500 steps improves almost every metric on every task. Reducing further to 50 50 improves PSNR and SSIM again, reaching the best values in the table on four of the five FFHQ tasks, while LPIPS and FID degrade moderately: coarser discretization accumulates less stochasticity, moving the sampler toward the posterior mean, which distortion metrics reward and perceptual metrics penalize. A 20 × 20\times reduction in inference cost is therefore available at a bounded perceptual cost, and a 2 × 2\times reduction at none.

sections.heading: Where SIMCA does not help.
sections.text: On ImageNet Gaussian deblurring, SIMCA trails the strongest baselines on every metric, reaching 25.28 25.28 dB against 28.06 28.06 for DDNM, and the same pattern appears on AFHQ-Cat deblurring and denoising. The improvement over DPS is the largest in the table, from 20.31 20.31 to 25.28 25.28 dB, so the residual gap reflects a Gaussian likelihood that is genuinely limiting on these operators.

sections.heading: Calibration set size.
sections.text: Table 5 varies the number of calibration images on FFHQ random and box inpainting. A single image already suffices. This is expected, since only two scalars are fitted per time step while each image contributes a full-dimensional inner product. Calibration is correspondingly cheap: solving for one weight pair takes 0.11 0.11 s from a single image and 6.76 6.76 s from one hundred, so a full schedule is obtained in seconds to minutes.

sections.heading: Simulation-free versus simulation-based calibration.
sections.text: Table 5 compares the two strategies of Section 4 on FFHQ random inpainting. Both improve substantially on the uncalibrated sampler. SIMCA is nonetheless uniformly better, with the largest margin on the perceptual metrics: for DPS, LPIPS falls from 0.103 0.103 to 0.069 0.069 and FID from 33.71 33.71 to 19.16 19.16 , a 43 % 43\% reduction for the same number of samples, and the same ordering holds for Π \Pi GDM and TMPD.

sections.text: Table 5 also compares different measurement-consistency terms: the isotropic Gaussian likelihood of DPS which all other experiments are based on (see Eq. 8 ), the pseudoinverse-based covariance correction of Π \Pi GDM, and the Tweedie moment projection of TMPD. Uncalibrated, they span 25.10 25.10 to 27.89 27.89 dB and 0.156 0.156 to 0.248 0.248 LPIPS, in the order the literature reports. After simulation-based calibration they become nearly indistinguishable: 32.91 32.91 , 32.97 32.97 , and 32.84 32.84 dB, with LPIPS of 0.069 0.069 , 0.069 0.069 , and 0.070 0.070 . sections.heading: Sampler and discretization.
sections.text: Recalibrating SIMCA for four samplers across seven step counts (Appendix E ) shows two patterns. Stochastic samplers dominate the deterministic ones at every budget. They also degrade differently: DDPM improves in PSNR down to 50 50 steps and only fails below 20 20 , whereas Euler-Maruyama collapses below 100 100 steps, losing 14 14 dB by 20 20 . Each cell is calibrated at its own discretization, which is what makes the low-step regime accessible.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduced SIMCA, a simple and principled offline strategy for tuning guidance weights in training-free posterior sampling. By exploiting the least-squares structure of conditional score- and flow-matching objectives, our method reduces guidance optimization to a two-dimensional linear least-squares problem at each sampling step. The resulting weights are optimized once for a given inverse problem setting, without retraining or fine-tuning the underlying generative model. Evaluated across four datasets and multiple inverse problems, using both diffusion- and flow-matching methods, our approach consistently matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

sections.heading: Use of AI tools
sections.text: In this work, we used a large language model to aid and polish writing. Its use was limited to rephrasing and condensing author-written text, drafting figure and table captions, and assisting with LaTeX formatting. We did not use generative AI tools for research ideation, for deriving or verifying the theoretical results, or for writing the code used in our experiments.

sections.heading: Control formulation.
sections.text: Li & Pereira (2024) derive a controller that recovers the idealized posterior sampling equation as a special case. Such methods optimize a control signal of full dimension, which requires differentiating through the sampling dynamics at substantial cost. This places them outside the regime we target, where a practitioner needs the guidance to be set in seconds for each new measurement setup.

sections.heading: Exposure bias.
sections.text: SIMCA addresses the mismatch between the forward marginals and the states visited at inference, known as exposure bias in diffusion models ( Ning et al., 2023 ; Ning et al., 2024 ) . Epsilon scaling ( Ning et al., 2024 ) rescales the network output with a hand-tuned schedule, an unconditional analogue of our prior weight a t a_{t} , which we instead obtain from an explicit criterion.

sections.heading: Appendix C Effect of the step count
sections.text: Figures 5 to 9 show SIMCA reconstructions at K = 1000 K=1000 , 500 500 and 50 50 steps, recalibrated at each discretization, on the five diffusion tasks. On the four well-posed operators (Gaussian deblurring, motion deblurring, super-resolution, random inpainting) the three columns are visually almost indistinguishable, which is the qualitative counterpart of the metric behaviour reported in Section 5.2 : reducing the budget twentyfold leaves reconstruction quality essentially unchanged. Box inpainting behaves differently, and instructively so. There the three budgets produce visibly different completions of the masked region, since that region is not determined by the measurement, while the unmasked part remains identical across columns. The step count therefore acts as a choice among plausible posterior samples rather than as a loss of fidelity, and the 50 50 -step reconstructions are no less plausible than the 1000 1000 -step ones, consistent with their higher PSNR and slightly worse FID. sections.heading: Appendix D Robustness to the backbone and the sampler.
sections.text: In Tab. 2 and Tab. 3 , two comparisons isolate what the gains depend on. First, in the flow-matching experiments, the OT-coupled and independently coupled backbones behave almost identically once calibrated, differing by at most 0.2 0.2 dB and 0.002 0.002 LPIPS on CelebA. Second, the renoising sampler outperforms the plain Euler integrator by 3.7 3.7 dB on CelebA random inpainting and 3.0 3.0 dB on box inpainting. This matches the deterministic-sampler penalty of Section 5.3 and is a property of the sampler rather than of calibration: the Euler rows still improve on most flow matching baselines.

sections.heading: Backbones and protocols.
sections.text: For diffusion, we use the pixel-space DDPM checkpoints for FFHQ and ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 released by ( Chung et al., 2022a ) , following the evaluation protocol of DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . For flow matching, we adopt the setup of Flower ( Pourya et al., 2026 ) , using the same U-Net velocity networks trained on CelebA and AFHQ-Cat. We evaluate both the OT-coupled network and its independently coupled variant, allowing us to assess calibration across two distinct pretrained velocity fields.

sections.heading: Datasets and metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate on 100 held-out images per dataset: FFHQ and ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 for diffusion, CelebA at 128 × 128 128\times 128 and AFHQ-Cat at 256 × 256 256\times 256 for flow matching. Images are scaled to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] for sampling and noise levels are expressed on this scale. We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) on both benchmarks, and FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) on the diffusion benchmark, averaged over individual images.

sections.heading: Inverse problems.
sections.text: On the diffusion side we consider super-resolution ( × 4 \times 4 bicubic downsampling), Gaussian deblurring ( 61 × 61 61\times 61 kernel, intensity 3.0 3.0 ), motion deblurring ( 61 × 61 61\times 61 kernel, intensity 0.5 0.5 ), box inpainting ( 128 × 128 128\times 128 central mask), and random inpainting ( 70 % 70\% masking rate), with additive white Gaussian noise of standard deviation σ m = 0.05 \sigma_{m}=0.05 . On the flow-matching side we consider the five tasks of the Flower benchmark, with operators and noise levels unchanged: denoising, Gaussian deblurring, super-resolution, random inpainting, and box inpainting.

Bordeaux, CNRS, BINP) Affiliation: Bordeaux, France Abstract Training-free posterior sampling methods, also known as Plug-and-Play methods, leverage pretrained unconditional diffusion or flow-matching models to solve inverse problems. Most existing approaches rely on guidance weights to balance, at each time step, prior information from the unconditional score or velocity network with measurement consistency, yet the tuning of these weights is often not discussed and is largely left to heuristics. We introduce a simple and principled offline strategy for automatically tuning these guidance weights. Our key observation is that, at each time step, the conditional denoising score-matching objective for diffusion models, or the conditional flow-matching objective for flow-matching models, is a least-squares objective. Therefore, when the conditional prediction is expressed as a weighted sum of the unconditional network output and a measurement-guidance term, optimizing over these weights reduces to a two-dimensional linear least-squares problem. The resulting time-dependent guidance weights can be optimized offline for a given measurement operator, noise level and sampler at the cost of a single minibatch of sampling trajectories, without retraining or fine-tuning the pretrained generative model. Instantiated with the standard Tweedie-based measurement-consistency term, our approach improves posterior sampling and achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction performance across diffusion- and flow-matching-based methods. Moreover, the optimized guidance weights enable diffusion samplers to reduce the number of sampling steps from 1000 to 50 with no significant degradation in reconstruction quality. Code will be made available. 1 Introduction Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Karras et al., 2022 ; Song & Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020 ; Song & Ermon, 2020 ) and flow matching models ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu, 2022 ; Tong et al., 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) have emerged as dominant families of iterative generative models, achieving remarkable success in synthesizing high-fidelity samples across a wide range of data modalities. However, training these models remains computationally expensive and can require substantial computational resources and time. In inverse problems, where the exact measurement operator and noise characteristics often depend on the acquisition setting specified at inference time, retraining or fine-tuning a generative model for each new acquisition setting is often impractical. Practitioners instead commonly rely on training-free methods ( Chung et al., 2022a ; Song et al., 2023 ; Boys et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Martin et al., 2025 ) , also referred to as Plug-and-Play methods. These methods leverage unconditionally pretrained generative models to perform approximate posterior sampling without requiring additional training for different measurement operators or noise levels. Most existing training-free methods ( Chung et al., 2022a ; Song et al., 2023 ; Boys et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Martin et al., 2025 ) incorporate a measurement-consistency step at each time step to modify the unconditional sampling direction, thereby steering the sampling trajectory toward samples consistent with the measurement. Repeating this procedure throughout the sampling process yields a sample from the approximate posterior distribution. Such methods usually rely on guidance weights to balance, at each time step, the prior information provided by the unconditional score or velocity network against measurement consistency. However, the tuning of these weights is often not discussed and is largely left to heuristics. In practice, the measurement setup may frequently change, for instance by modifying the number or locations of sensors, or their internal acquisition settings ( Donoho, 2006 ) . Such modifications require the guidance weights to be re-tuned, introducing an additional and time-consuming hyperparameter optimization step. Consequently, the need to tune guidance weights represents a key practical bottleneck of existing training-free posterior sampling methods. This motivates the development of a strategy to automatically and efficiently determine appropriate guidance weights for a given measurement setup. Importantly, such a strategy must introduce negligible computational overhead. From a practitioner’s perspective, guidance selection should take only a few seconds, ruling out iterative optimizers ( e.g. gradient descent, etc.) that require repeated ODE/SDE integrations. In this paper, we introduce a simple and principled offline calibration strategy for automatically tuning time-dependent guidance weights. Our contributions are as follows: • We make the key observation that, at each time step, the conditional denoising score-matching objective for diffusion models and the conditional flow-matching objective for flow-matching models are least-squares objectives. Therefore, when the conditional prediction is expressed as a weighted sum of the unconditional network output and a measurement-guidance term, optimizing these weights reduces to a two-dimensional linear least-squares problem. This yields a highly efficient, simulation-free strategy for calibrating time-dependent guidance weights. • While theoretically grounded, the simulation-free calibration strategy does not guarantee improved posterior sampling trajectories, since neither the measurement-consistency term nor the unconditional network is necessarily optimal. To address this limitation, we propose a greedy SIMulation-based CAlibration strategy (SIMCA), which sequentially calibrates the guidance weight at each time step while keeping the weights calibrated at previous time steps fixed. SIMCA requires only a single minibatch of sampling trajectories, making it practical for tuning time-dependent guidance weights in a given measurement setup. • We empirically demonstrate that SIMCA, instantiated with the standard Tweedie-based measurement-consistency term, matches or surpasses state-of-the-art training-free methods across multiple inverse problems and datasets, using both diffusion and flow-matching backbones. • We further show that SIMCA enables diffusion samplers to reduce the number of sampling steps from 1000 to 50, a × 20 \times 20 reduction in inference cost, without significant degradation in reconstruction quality. 2 Background on training-free posterior sampling Unconditional diffusion models and (Gaussian) flow-matching. Additive training-free samplers weight their measurement-consistency term either heuristically, as the residual-normalized step of DPS ( Chung et al., 2022a ) and the hand-set schedules of flow-based samplers ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Martin et al., 2025 ) , or through a Gaussian model of the denoising posterior, as in Π \Pi GDM ( Song et al., 2023 ) , TMPD ( Boys et al., 2023 ) , their refinements ( Peng et al., 2024 ) , and their flow counterpart OT-ODE ( Pokle et al., 2024 ) . The latter derive the weight from an assumed posterior covariance rather than tuning it, and thereby improve both the measurement term and its effective scale; our ablations suggest that this second effect accounts for much of their benefit (Section 5.3 ). What none of them does is fit the weight to a criterion measurable from data, and all fix the weight of the pretrained field to one. Adaptive guidance. Time-varying weights have been studied mainly for classifier-free guidance ( Malarz et al., 2025 ) , where the weight trades sample quality against conditioning fidelity and, having no reference value, is set heuristically. In training-free inverse problems the guided field approximates a well-defined conditional field, so its approximation error can be measured against the tractable target of Eq. 5 and minimized in closed form rather than tuned. SIMCA requires only a single minibatch of sampling trajectories, making it practical for tuning time-dependent guidance weights for a given measurement setup. Once calibrated, the guidance weights are fixed and introduce no inference-time overhead. Recalibration. The guidance weights depend on the measurement operator 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , the noise level σ m \sigma_{m} , the measurement-consistency term 𝐟 \mathbf{f} , the pretrained unconditional network 𝐮 𝜽 \mathbf{u}_{\bm{\theta}} , the sampler Φ \Phi , and the number of timesteps. They must therefore be recomputed whenever any of these components changes. Since each recalibration requires only one offline pass, practitioners can efficiently adapt the guidance weights to different measurement setups. Compatibility. Our calibration procedure applies to any method whose guidance takes the additive form in Eq. equation 8 . It requires no retraining, architectural changes, or modifications to the sampler. 5 Experiments 5.1 Experimental Setup Backbones and protocols.
